title: The Rectory to the Looking-Glass: the Mathematician, the Camera, and Alice
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Daresbury, the birth at the parsonage
stops.campa: At the Old Parsonage of Newton-by-Daresbury, in the flat Cheshire country between Warrington and the Mersey, a son is born to the Reverend Charles Dodgson and Frances Jane Lutwidge, third child and eldest boy of what will be eleven. They name him Charles Lutwidge, doubling the family names, and christen him in his father's church of All Saints. The parsonage stands a mile and a half from the village, isolated among fields; the boy grows up among his sisters, snails and toads for company, and a father who is at once curate, classicist, and the first mathematician he will know. The house burns down in 1883; the church keeps the register.
suggested_refs: The 1935 Geoffrey Webb memorial window in the Daniell Chapel of All Saints', Daresbury, showing Carroll and Alice
sources: Morton N. Cohen, Lewis Carroll: A Biography (1995)

stops.name: Croft-on-Tees, the impresario of the nursery
stops.campa: At eleven he moves with the household to Croft-on-Tees, on the Yorkshire bank of the river, where his father has been given a comfortable living and a rambling rectory. Here Charles becomes impresario of the nursery: he writes, edits, and illustrates family magazines, Useful and Instructive Poetry and later The Rectory Umbrella, builds marionette theatres and railway games for his siblings, and keeps the whole tribe amused with puzzles and parody. The verbal play that will one day open under another name begins at this table, for an audience of sisters who see in it only their brother's ordinary cleverness.
suggested_refs: St Peter's rectory, Croft-on-Tees, family seat of the Dodgsons for a quarter-century

stops.name: Richmond, the first school away from home
stops.campa: At twelve he is sent ten miles from home to board at Richmond School under James Tate, his first schooling away from the rectory. He is homesick and writes constantly for his sisters, but the verdict that will follow him through every classroom is already in: his master reports a boy of uncommon promise, especially in mathematics, and warns only of a certain impatience with slow or crooked reasoning. He construes Latin and ciphers figures with equal ease, and waits, not altogether happily, to be sent on to a public school.
suggested_refs: The Lewis Carroll Society of North America chronology of the Richmond and Rugby years
sources: Lewis Carroll Society of North America chronology

stops.name: Rugby, three years he would not repeat
stops.campa: Rugby he will remember as three years no earthly consideration would make him live again: the dormitory's lack of privacy, the casual brutality among boys, a shy and stammering scholar's daily ordeal. Yet he excels without visible effort. The mathematics master R. B. Mayor calls him the most promising boy of his age to arrive at the school in years, and he carries off prize after prize in classics and divinity besides. He leaves Rugby at the end of 1849 with a first-rate record.
suggested_refs: R. B. Mayor's report on the young Dodgson's mathematical promise at Rugby

stops.name: Christ Church, matriculation and the loss of his mother
stops.campa: He matriculates at Christ Church on the twenty-third of May 1850 and goes into residence the following January, taking rooms he will keep, in one set or another, for the whole of the rest of his life. His mother dies within months of his arrival, of what the family records as inflammation of the brain, a grief he never puts on paper. He reads mathematics and classics, wins a first in mathematical moderations in 1852, and in 1854 takes first-class honours in the Final Honours School of Mathematics, at the head of his list.
suggested_refs: Dodgson's rooms at the north-west corner of Tom Quad, Christ Church

stops.name: Ripon, the griffin and the rabbit hole
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the misericord carvings are attested and Dodgson was present at Ripon, but any link to the rabbit hole is Ripon tradition, not documented by him
stops.campa: His father, made a canon of Ripon in 1852, brings the family to the cathedral city for three months of each year, and the young undergraduate spends his vacations among its stones. In the choir a misericord shows a griffin chasing a rabbit down into its hole, and under the stalls a procession of grotesques that Ripon's own tradition, long after, will offer as a seed of the rabbit hole and the creatures below it. Whether the boy noticed them, no diary says. He was certainly in the building, and the carvings were certainly there.
suggested_refs: Ripon Cathedral, 'Lewis Carroll Carvings and Connection'
sources: Ripon Cathedral, 'Lewis Carroll Carvings and Connection'
Daresbury Lewis Carroll Society, 'The Ripon Connection'

stops.name: Whitby, the first work in print
stops.campa: At twenty-two he spends a summer reading party on the North Yorkshire coast at Whitby, coaching under the mathematician Bartholomew Price among the red roofs and the harbour. Here he writes a comic poem, The Lady of the Ladle, naming the Royal Hotel and the Marine Parade outright, and it appears in the Whitby Gazette: the first of his writing to reach print, years before the pseudonym exists. The sea town takes a mild local pride in it; the undergraduate takes his mathematics back to Oxford and a first-class degree waiting the next year.
suggested_refs: The Whitby Gazette printing of 'The Lady of the Ladle,' 1854

stops.name: Christ Church, the lectureship and the pen name
stops.campa: In 1855 Christ Church appoints him to its Mathematical Lectureship, the post from which he teaches undergraduates for twenty-six years, until 1881. The salary is modest and the duties heavy: hundreds of pupils drilled through Euclid and algebra by a lecturer most of them find dry. He keeps meticulous records, devises teaching aids, and privately finds the work wearying. The next year, writing for the comic magazine The Train, he needs a name to publish under, and from Charles Lutwidge, turned into Latin and back again, comes Lewis Carroll.
suggested_refs: The poem 'Solitude,' The Train, March 1856, first work signed Lewis Carroll
sources: Lewis Carroll Society of North America

stops.name: Oxford, the acquaintance with Ruskin
stops.campa: In 1857 he meets John Ruskin, the critic not yet installed in Oxford's Slade chair but already the most listened-to voice in English art, and the acquaintance holds for decades. Ruskin later gives drawing lessons to Alice Liddell and advises Dodgson, discouragingly, on his own hopes as a draughtsman; Dodgson photographs him and keeps his books. It is one of a widening circle of eminent friendships, Tennyson, the Rossettis, Millais, that the shy mathematician assembles with a photographer's patient persistence, uneasy about his own growing fame yet drawn to everyone else's.
suggested_refs: Ruskin's drawing lessons to Alice Liddell, recalled in the Liddell family papers

stops.name: The Deanery, the camera and the Liddell children
stops.campa: The year 1856 brings two things that shape the rest of his life. Henry Liddell arrives as Dean of Christ Church with his family, among them three small daughters, Lorina, Alice, and Edith, who live inside the college walls. And Dodgson, under the spell of his uncle Skeffington Lutwidge and his friend Reginald Southey, buys a camera. Photography is then a labour of wet collodion plates, timed exposures, and a portable darkroom; he masters it with a mathematician's exactness and becomes, within a few years, one of the finest amateur portraitists in England. His favourite sitters are children, and the Deanery garden lies next door.
suggested_refs: The Liddell children photographed at the Deanery through the 1850s and 1860s

stops.name: Farringford, Tennyson at the mowing
stops.campa: In 1859 he calls uninvited at Farringford, Tennyson's house on the Isle of Wight, and finds the Poet Laureate mowing his own lawn in a wide hat. The intrusion is forgiven; Dodgson photographs the Tennyson family and visits the Freshwater circle repeatedly over the following years. He is a connoisseur of other men's celebrity, pursuing the great with his camera and his calling card while shrinking from any notice of his own. Tennyson he admires without quite liking, and the acquaintance cools, as several of his famous friendships do, into a wary civility.
suggested_refs: Dodgson's portraits of the Tennyson family, Farringford

stops.name: Dimbola Lodge, two cameras disagreeing
stops.campa: Down the lane at Freshwater lives Julia Margaret Cameron, who takes up the same camera a few years after him and turns it to soft-focused, heroic portraiture utterly unlike his crisp documentary eye. They exhibit together, lend each other sitters, and privately disagree about everything: he thinks her blurred saints taken purposely out of focus; she thinks his sharpness mere mechanism. In the 1870s Cameron photographs Alice Liddell grown into a young woman, the same face he had fixed as a child a decade before, by a wholly opposite art.
suggested_refs: The joint Dodgson-Cameron exhibition at Dimbola Lodge

stops.name: Oxford, ordained deacon and no further
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of December 1861 he is ordained deacon in the Church of England, as the terms of his Christ Church studentship require. The further step to priest he never takes. A stammer he fears in the pulpit, a growing taste for the theatre that a priest could not indulge, and scruples he keeps mostly to himself hold him back; and Dean Liddell, bending the college's own rule, lets him remain a senior member without proceeding to orders. He stays a deacon for the rest of his life, Reverend but never quite a clergyman, preaching rarely and reluctantly.
suggested_refs: The Christ Church studentship rule on ordination, waived in Dodgson's case

stops.name: Folly Bridge, the boat is hired
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the outing; the single-afternoon origin is contested by the weather record
stops.campa: On the fourth of July 1862 he hires a boat at Folly Bridge, below the city, and rows upriver with his friend Robinson Duckworth and the three Liddell sisters, Lorina thirteen, Alice ten, Edith eight. The day he will later gild as a cloudless golden afternoon was, the Oxford weather records insist, cool and wet; scholars still argue whether the whole tale was told on this single outing or assembled across many. The boat turns up the Isis toward Godstow, and somewhere between the oars Alice asks for a story.
suggested_refs: The Folly Bridge plaque marking the start of the 1862 river party

stops.name: Godstow, the story written out for Alice
stops.campa: Five miles up, the party lands near the ruined nunnery at Godstow to shelter and take tea, and here the improvised tale reaches its first end: a bored girl named Alice who follows a waistcoated rabbit down a hole into a country where logic runs mad. Alice Liddell begs him to write it out for her. He will, in a small hand with his own pen drawings, as Alice's Adventures Under Ground, and give her the manuscript two years on. The afternoon that may never quite have happened as he tells it becomes the origin every later reader is handed.
suggested_refs: The manuscript 'Alice's Adventures Under Ground,' given to Alice Liddell in 1864

stops.name: Christ Church, the rupture in the cut diary
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the diary page is missing and the cause is disputed among biographers
stops.campa: In June 1863 something breaks between Dodgson and the Liddell household, and for a time he is no longer welcome at the Deanery. The page of his diary that would say why was later cut out by an unknown family hand, and the silence has drawn a century of guesses: gossip about the children's governess, a supposed attachment to the eldest sister Lorina, even a legend that he proposed marriage to the eleven-year-old Alice. A niece's summary of the missing pages, found and published in 1996, points to gossip rather than any proposal. The record is a hole; the theories are what rush in to fill it.
suggested_refs: 'The Cut Pages in Diary' document (published 1996)
Karoline Leach, In the Shadow of the Dreamchild
sources: carroll-myth.wild-reality.net, 'Is the missing page about a marriage proposal?'
Morton N. Cohen, Lewis Carroll: A Biography (1995)

stops.name: Cheyne Walk, photographing the Rossettis
stops.campa: On the seventh of October 1863 he carries his camera to 16 Cheyne Walk in Chelsea, the house of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and photographs the painter's family in the garden among the exotic animals Rossetti keeps there. A shower spoils the planned group negative, leaving Christina Rossetti with a single print. From it grows a correspondence between the mathematician and the poet of Goblin Market that runs into the 1890s; he sends her his Alice books, she sends him her verses, and each reads the other's descents into strange countries without ever quite saying so.
stops.quote: the famous ghost story which has interested us all
stops.quote_source: Christina Rossetti to C. L. Dodgson, 17 November 1882 (victorianweb.org)
suggested_refs: The Rossetti family group, National Portrait Gallery NPG P56
Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market (1862), read as a likely influence on Wonderland's descent
sources: National Portrait Gallery, 'The Rossetti Family' (NPG P56)
Bonhams, Dodgson photograph of the Rossetti family, 1863
victorianweb.org, letters of Carroll and Christina Rossetti

stops.name: Christ Church, Alice goes to the world
stops.campa: In 1865 Macmillan publishes Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the river tale grown to book length, with forty-two wood engravings by John Tenniel after Dodgson's own designs. The first printing is recalled over the quality of the plates and reissued the next year; from there it never goes out of print. A deacon's and lecturer's private amusement for three real girls becomes the book that remakes English children's writing, cutting loose the moralising tale and letting nonsense stand on its own logic. Lewis Carroll, the name on the spine, now belongs to the world; Charles Dodgson keeps teaching Euclid.
suggested_refs: Gilles Deleuze, Logique du sens (1969), which builds its theory of sense and nonsense on the Alice books
Charly Garcia's 'Cancion de Alicia en el pais' (Seru Giran, 1980), an Argentine allegory of life under the dictatorship
Silvina Ocampo's recollection of Alicia en el pais de las maravillas among the books of her childhood; the Antologia de la literatura fantastica (Borges, Bioy Casares, Ocampo, 1940)
Maurice Sendak, who kept a photograph of Alice Liddell by his desk
sources: Lewis Carroll Society of North America

stops.name: Christ Church, Euclid's defender at the tea-table
stops.date_confidence: The Dynamics of a Particle appeared in 1865; the quaternion reading of the Mad Tea-Party is a later scholarly reconstruction, explicitly contested, with no proof Dodgson studied Hamilton
stops.campa: In his own mathematics he is a thoroughgoing conservative, loyal to Euclid and wary of the new symbolic algebras unsettling the subject. In 1865 he prints The Dynamics of a Particle, a squib satirising an Oxford curriculum fight in mock-geometric form. Later readers, taking Wonderland back through this temper, find in the Mad Tea-Party a parody of William Rowan Hamilton's quaternions, the four-part algebra of 1843 whose multiplication abandons its old obedience. Specialists caution that nothing proves he studied Hamilton at all; the kinship of temper is attested, the particular satire a reconstruction.
suggested_refs: Melanie Bayley, 'Algebra in Wonderland'; 'Alice without quaternions,' BSHM Bulletin (2022), which qualifies the reading

segments.name: The Determinant and the Road East

stops.name: London, the condensation of determinants
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of May 1866 the Royal Society hears a paper by the Christ Church lecturer on a new way of evaluating determinants, printed that year as Condensation of Determinants. The method, now called Dodgson condensation, folds a square array down by a rule of two-by-two minors until one number remains, a mechanical recipe no one had set out so plainly. Only in the next century do mathematicians see how far it reaches, into the Desnanot-Jacobi identity and the combinatorics of alternating-sign matrices.
suggested_refs: Dodgson's 'Condensation of Determinants,' Proceedings of the Royal Society (1866)
sources: Thales and Friends, 'Lewis Carroll and His Telescoping Determinants'

stops.name: St Petersburg, the only journey abroad
stops.campa: In the summer of 1867 he makes the only journey of his life beyond western Europe, travelling to Russia with his friend Henry Liddon, who carries letters of Anglican goodwill to the Orthodox Church. St Petersburg is their first great stop: the broad Neva, the gilded spire of the Peter and Paul fortress, services in a language and a liturgy wholly strange to a Church of England deacon. He keeps a diary of the trip, published only in 1935, that dwells as readily on hotel dinners and the difficulty of Russian words as on cathedrals.
suggested_refs: Lewis Carroll, The Russian Journal (written 1867, published 1935)

stops.name: Moscow, the telescoping towers
stops.campa: At Moscow the two Englishmen walk the Kremlin and Red Square, and Dodgson sets down the domes and the colour with an almost bewildered relish, a city, he writes, of conical towers that telescope out of one another. They are received on the fringe of Liddon's real errand, the slow diplomacy between Canterbury and the Russian Church, with Dodgson along as companion and witness rather than envoy. He buys icons and photographs nothing, his camera left in England.
suggested_refs: Dodgson's Moscow entries in The Russian Journal
sources: rbth.com, 'Moscow: the city in Lewis Carroll's footsteps'

stops.name: Nizhny Novgorod, the farthest point
stops.campa: They push east to Nizhny Novgorod for its great summer fair, among the largest markets of the Russian empire, a plain of booths and goods from Persia and central Asia spread along the Volga and the Oka. It is the farthest point of the whole journey, deeper into the continent than any other errand of his life will take him. Tatar traders, tea by the chest, mosques beside onion domes: he writes it all down in the same even hand, then turns the party back toward the west.
suggested_refs: The Nizhny Novgorod fair, described in The Russian Journal

stops.name: Sergiev Posad, the gold of Orthodoxy
stops.campa: On the way back they visit the Trinity Lavra of Saint Sergius at Sergiev Posad, the walled mother-house of Russian monasticism, where Liddon's errand of church to church is most at home. Dodgson stands among the relics and the chanting monks, a deacon of a reformed church inside the dense gold of Orthodoxy, and takes it in with curiosity rather than devotion. The nine-week journey will give him nothing he obviously uses in his books, no rabbit hole, no looking-glass; only the diary, and a lifetime's single excursion outside the familiar.
suggested_refs: Liddon's account of the Anglican-Orthodox mission of 1867

stops.name: Oxford, the cipher he thought unbreakable
stops.campa: Back in Oxford, in 1868, he publishes in a children's magazine The Alphabet Cipher, a short method for secret writing by a sliding square of letters keyed to a chosen word. It is, in mechanism, the polyalphabetic cipher of the sixteenth-century Frenchman Blaise de Vigenere, reinvented by a don who delighted in ciphers, acrostics, and secret hands; Carroll calls it unbreakable. He is wrong, and freshly wrong: Friedrich Kasiski had published a general attack on just such ciphers in 1863, and Charles Babbage had quietly broken them a decade earlier still.
suggested_refs: Carroll, 'The Alphabet Cipher' (1868); Kasiski's 1863 attack on polyalphabetic ciphers

stops.name: Christ Church, the philologist's joke
stops.date_confidence: attested as to Muller's chair and Dodgson's reading of his Lectures; the philological reading of the nonsense tongue is scholarly interpretation
stops.campa: His Christ Church years run beside those of Max Muller, the German-born philologist who holds Oxford's first Chair of Comparative Philology from 1868 and makes the science of language a public fascination. Dodgson reads Muller's Lectures on the Science of Language and shares his common-room world for decades; scholars trace in the nonsense tongue of the Alice books, the portmanteau word, the solemn etymologies of invented creatures, an ear tuned by exactly this philology, which treats words as living things with histories.
suggested_refs: Max Muller, Lectures on the Science of Language; 'Lewis Carroll and the Private Life of Words,' Review of English Studies
sources: Review of English Studies, 'Lewis Carroll and the Private Life of Words'

stops.name: Oxford, through the looking-glass
stops.campa: In 1871 Macmillan brings out Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There, the second Alice, built not on a pack of cards but on a chess game whose moves run as a diagram at the front. Tenniel illustrates again, over the author's exacting corrections. Into it goes Jabberwocky, a poem in words that do not exist yet parse perfectly, and the White Knight, gentle, inventive, forever sliding off his horse, in whom many readers see Dodgson's own portrait. The book sells on sight and fixes Alice, for good, as two books rather than one.
suggested_refs: The chess-problem frontispiece of Through the Looking-Glass

stops.name: Christ Church, the studio on the leads
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the studio and the photographic record; the interpretation of the child photographs is unresolved and disputed among scholars
stops.campa: In 1872 he has a glass-roofed studio built on the leads above his Christ Church rooms, so that weather no longer governs his sittings, and stocks it with costumes borrowed from the theatre for his tableaux. Across a quarter-century at the camera he makes some three thousand photographs; more than half are of children, most clothed and posed in fancy dress with parents present, a few, by arrangement with their mothers, nude in the manner Victorian art photography then thought innocent. From this studio comes both his name as a portraitist and, a century on, the long unsettled argument over what the pictures mean.
stops.quote: I am fond of children (except boys).
stops.quote_source: Lewis Carroll, letter to Kathleen Eschwege, 24 October 1879 (ed. Cohen)
suggested_refs: Roger Taylor and Edward Wakeling's catalogue of Dodgson's photographs; Cohen (1995) and Leach's revisionist reading on the child photographs
sources: statesman.com, 'A tribute to Lewis Carroll's photography'

stops.name: Clarendon Press, the mathematics of voting
stops.date_confidence: attested; often misdated to 1884, which is instead the date of his separate proportional-representation work
stops.campa: In March 1876 the Clarendon Press prints, marked not yet published, his pamphlet A Method of Taking Votes on More than Two Issues, worrying at how a committee should choose when three or more options divide it. He proposes picking the option that beats every other head to head, and when none does, the one reachable by the fewest reversals of preference, a rule now called Dodgson's method. He is doing, decades early and without the name, the mathematics of social choice. In 1884 he returns to it in The Principles of Parliamentary Representation, arguing for proportional representation on the same analytic nerve.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi, Tovey and Trick, 'Lewis Carroll's 1876 voting system' (J. ACM, 1989)

stops.name: Guildford, the hunting of the Snark
stops.campa: In 1876 he publishes The Hunting of the Snark, a long nonsense ballad of a crew, each of whose names begins with B, sailing to hunt a creature no one can describe, which may turn out to be a Boojum. Henry Holiday illustrates it. Carroll insists for the rest of his life that it means nothing he can explain, deflecting every interpretation with the same patient refusal; readers have hunted allegories of death, happiness, and the absolute through it ever since. It is dedicated, in an acrostic, to a real child, Gertrude Chataway.
suggested_refs: Henry Holiday's illustrations to The Hunting of the Snark (1876)

stops.name: Oxford, Euclid put on trial
stops.campa: In 1879, under his own name, he publishes Euclid and His Modern Rivals, a defence of Euclid's Elements against the reform textbooks crowding it out of the schoolroom, cast, improbably, as a stage comedy in which the ghost of Euclid cross-examines his would-be replacements one by one. The joke carries a real argument: that for teaching and examining geometry, one agreed text and one fixed order of propositions serve better than many. It is the Oxford lecturer and the author of Alice in a single book, a point of hard pedagogy made by putting a dead Greek geometer on trial before an audience.
stops.quote: The object of this little book is to furnish evidence, first, that it is essential, for the purpose of teaching or examining in elementary Geometry, to employ one text-book only.
stops.quote_source: Charles L. Dodgson, preface to Euclid and His Modern Rivals (1879)
suggested_refs: Euclid and His Modern Rivals (1879), full text at schnark.github.io/lewis-carroll
sources: Euclid and His Modern Rivals (1879), preface

segments.name: The Society, the Logic, and Guildford

stops.name: Christ Church, the camera laid down
stops.campa: In the summer of 1880, after some twenty-four years and three thousand plates, he gives up photography altogether, the rooftop studio's endless chemistry and upkeep too much to sustain beside his writing and teaching. He never takes it up again. Much of his earlier work he deliberately destroys or returns to sitters; roughly three in five of his negatives do not survive, and the catalogue later assembled by Roger Taylor and Edward Wakeling must reconstruct the whole from what is left.
suggested_refs: Roger Taylor and Edward Wakeling, Lewis Carroll, Photographer (catalogue)
sources: Taylor and Wakeling, catalogue of Dodgson's photographs

stops.name: Christ Church, the Society and the force allied to electricity
stops.date_confidence: SPR membership attested in the Proceedings lists 1883-1889; the separate claim of Theosophical Society membership is unsubstantiated and treated here as a likely conflation with the SPR
stops.campa: From at least 1883 his name stands in the published membership lists of the Society for Psychical Research, founded the year before to weigh thought-reading, apparitions, and the seance on scientific terms. He is no credulous spiritualist: writing to a friend in 1882 he sets thought-reading not among ghosts but among natural forces, something allied to electricity and nerve-force. The claim that he also joined Helena Blavatsky's Theosophical Society finds no roll, letter, or record behind it; what the documents show is the Society for Psychical Research, and a reader's interest in theosophy's books, never a theosophist's card.
stops.quote: All seems to point to the existence of a natural force, allied to electricity and nerve-force, by which brain can act on brain.
stops.quote_source: Lewis Carroll, letter to James Langton Clarke, 4 December 1882 (Psi Encyclopedia, citing Cohen, ed., The Letters of Lewis Carroll)
suggested_refs: SPR Proceedings membership lists, 1883-1889; the Theosophical Society (founded 1875), which no record places him in
sources: Lewis Carroll Society of North America, 'Religion'

stops.name: Eastbourne, the second home by the sea
stops.date_confidence: residence attested across the summers 1877-1896; this stop is dated to a representative summer within that span
stops.campa: From 1877 he takes summer lodgings at 7 Lushington Road in Eastbourne, on the Sussex coast, and returns almost every year for the best part of two decades. Here, away from Oxford, he writes, walks the front, works at his logic and his puzzles, and makes friends among the children on the beach by the dozen. The seaside house becomes a second home more restful than the college; a blue plaque marks it now. His letters from Eastbourne are the letters of a man at ease, which the Oxford ones are not always.
suggested_refs: The blue plaque at 7 Lushington Road, Eastbourne
sources: johnnicholsons.com, 'What's in a name? Ask Lewis Carroll'

stops.name: Christ Church, the fairy kingdom and Esoteric Buddhism
stops.date_confidence: attested; the two volumes appeared in 1889 and 1893
stops.campa: His last long work is the two-volume Sylvie and Bruno, published in 1889 and finished in 1893, an ambitious, half-forgotten double novel that cuts between a Victorian drawing-room and a fairy kingdom, and between waking, trance, and an eerie state in between that the narrator tries to map. In its preface he borrows openly from theosophy, naming A. P. Sinnett's Esoteric Buddhism as a model for souls meeting by transfer of their immaterial essence. Here is the root of the theosophy rumour: a reader who used the movement's ideas in a novel, not a member whose name appears on its rolls.
stops.quote: by actual transference of their immaterial essence, such as we meet with in 'Esoteric Buddhism'
stops.quote_source: Lewis Carroll, preface to Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893)
suggested_refs: Sylvie and Bruno (1889) and Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893); A. P. Sinnett, Esoteric Buddhism
sources: Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893), preface, at etc.usf.edu/lit2go

stops.name: Christ Church chapel, the hymn foreseen
stops.date_confidence: attested; recorded in his own notebook
stops.campa: On the sixth of September 1891, sitting in the Christ Church chapel, he opens his hymn-book certain, for no reason he can give, that the number will be 416, and hears the curate a moment later announce hymn 416. He notes it down as really startling, suggestive of telepathy, one more private datum for the natural force he has argued for across the years. He weighs such things as a working member of his Society weighs them, neither dismissing them as conjuring nor crediting them to the dead, but filing them as evidence for a power of brain upon brain not yet understood.
stops.quote: I took my hymn-book, and said to myself (I have no idea why) 'it will be hymn 416'... the next minute, to hear the curate announce 'Hymn 416'!
stops.quote_source: Lewis Carroll, notebook, 6 September 1891 (Psi Encyclopedia; Wakeling, ed., Lewis Carroll's Diaries)
suggested_refs: Edward Wakeling, ed., Lewis Carroll's Diaries, vol. 8

stops.name: The Chestnuts, Guildford, the last work
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of January 1898 he dies of pneumonia following influenza at The Chestnuts, the Guildford house he had leased thirty years before for his unmarried sisters and visited to the end of his life. He is sixty-five, thirteen days short of his birthday. He had kept working to the last on the second part of his Symbolic Logic, the sequel to the Part I he had printed in 1896, the book of reasoning he meant for the young, and leaves it unfinished.
stops.quote: the power to detect fallacies, and to tear to pieces the flimsy illogical arguments, which you will so continually encounter in books, in newspapers, in speeches, and even in sermons
stops.quote_source: Lewis Carroll, preface to Symbolic Logic, Part I (1896)
suggested_refs: Symbolic Logic, Part I (1896), Project Gutenberg edition 28696

stops.name: The Mount, Guildford, the two names on one stone
stops.campa: Days later he is buried on the hillside of the Mount Cemetery above Guildford, after a quiet funeral at St Mary's, under a plain white cross his brothers and sisters raise over him near his aunt Lucy Lutwidge. The grave is marked Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, with the added line Lewis Carroll, the only place the two names are cut in the same stone. Pilgrims still climb to it. The dream of a golden afternoon ends on a Surrey hill, within sight of the town, under the real name and the made one together.
suggested_refs: The grave of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, Mount Cemetery, Guildford
